shows.title: The Heart of the Matter
shows.description:
Carrie Mae Weems has spent four decades using photography, text, video and installation to interrogate how images construct race, gender and power in American life, and this survey-style presentation gathers work spanning from her landmark "Kitchen Table Series" of the early 1990s through recent video pieces. The kitchen-table pictures, staged around a single table lit by one hanging bulb, remain some of the most quietly devastating images in American photography — a woman reading, arguing, applying makeup, raising a daughter, all performed by Weems herself as a stand-in for countless lives.

Alongside that early work, the show brings in Weems's ongoing "Museums" series, in which she photographs herself as a small dark silhouette facing the imposing façades of institutions like the Louvre — a wry, melancholy meditation on who gets to stand inside the canon and who is left looking at its doors. More recent video and photographic work, including pieces addressing preaching, protest and departure, extends her long-running interest in the performativity of Black public and private life.

Taken together, "The Heart of the Matter" traces a throughline in Weems's practice: an insistence that domestic intimacy and grand institutional history are part of the same story about visibility, exclusion and self-possession. It's a rare chance in Berlin to see the arc of one of contemporary photography's most influential bodies of work in one place.
shows.reception: Friday, September 11, 2026, 20:00–00:00 (joint opening with Kallinikou and Kriemann)

shows.title: Cliffs Among Dreams
shows.description:
Cypriot photographer Stelios Kallinikou builds his images around the specific, saturated light of the Eastern Mediterranean, and this exhibition brings together landscapes, portraits and still lifes shot around Cyprus's coastline and interior. Palm trees, flamingos, harbor gates and sun-bleached bays recur as motifs, rendered in a palette so intensely colored it almost tips into artifice — a way of looking at a place so familiar to the artist that ordinary scenery starts to feel like a stage set or a half-remembered dream.

Kallinikou's pictures sit in a lineage of Mediterranean color photography that treats the region's tourism-postcard beauty with real suspicion, using heightened saturation and careful, formal composition to ask what's underneath the picturesque surface — questions of displacement, borders and ecological pressure that shadow an island still divided by conflict. It's a body of work that rewards close, patient looking, and pairs well with the other photography-based shows opening the same week at C/O Berlin.
shows.reception: Friday, September 11, 2026, 20:00–00:00 (joint opening with Weems and Kriemann)

shows.title: Butterflies Flutter in the Fever of the Sun
shows.description:
Susanne Kriemann works at the intersection of photography and ecological research, and this exhibition (its German title translates roughly as "Butterflies Flutter in the Fever of the Sun") continues her long engagement with radioactive contamination and plant life. Her large-format photograms, made using pitchblende — the uranium-bearing ore mineral — as both subject and quasi co-author, expose sheet film to gamma radiation to produce ghostly, glowing images of plants like plantain, lupin, fern and broom that grow near former uranium mining sites.

The resulting pictures sit somewhere between botanical illustration and forensic evidence: delicate, almost floral compositions that are also documents of invisible, long-lived toxicity in the land. Kriemann has spent years researching the ecological aftermath of uranium mining in Central Europe, and this body of work extends that research into a quietly unsettling visual language, where beauty and contamination are impossible to separate.
shows.reception: Friday, September 11, 2026, 20:00–00:00 (joint opening with Weems and Kallinikou)

shows.title: Brassaï (1899–1984) Retrospektive
shows.description:
This retrospective surveys the career of Gyula Halász, the Hungarian-French photographer who took the name Brassaï after his hometown and became one of the defining chroniclers of interwar Paris. Working mostly at night with a large-format camera, he photographed the city's brothels, dance halls, opium dens and back-alley encounters alongside its fog-wrapped bridges and gaslit streets, publishing much of this material in his 1933 book "Paris de nuit," which effectively invented a whole photographic genre of nocturnal urban observation.

The exhibition, drawn from vintage prints, gives a sense of Brassaï's range beyond the nightlife pictures for which he's best known: portraits of friends and contemporaries in the Parisian art world (he moved in circles that included Picasso, Henry Miller and the Surrealists), graffiti studies that fascinated Surrealist writers for their raw, anonymous mark-making, and more intimate genre scenes shot in the city's bars and cafés. Brassaï approached the camera as a writer as much as an image-maker — Miller nicknamed him "the eye of Paris" — and his prints have a literary attentiveness to gesture and atmosphere that set him apart from more purely documentary contemporaries.

As a specialist in vintage photography, Galerie Berinson is well positioned to show this material in its original prints rather than later reproductions, which matters enormously for a photographer whose deep blacks and silvery highlights were central to his effects. It's a rare opportunity to see this much original Brassaï material together outside a museum context.

shows.title: the now and then
shows.dates_note: Venue's current-exhibition page gives only "Opening: 10 September, 6-9pm" with no stated closing date; saved with start date only.
shows.description:
Henrik Strömberg has spent two decades taking apart the language of photography and putting it back together as sculpture, glass, and installation, and the now and then continues that practice for Berlin Art Week. Rather than presenting straightforward images, Strömberg tends to treat the photograph as raw material — cutting, casting, and rebuilding it alongside found objects so that a picture becomes a physical, walk-around thing rather than a flat surface.

The Swedish, Berlin-based artist trained in fine art photography at FAMU in Prague and fine art at Camberwell in London, and that dual grounding shows in how comfortably the work moves between the documentary and the sculptural. Expect an installation that mixes glass, sculptural volumes, and photographic fragments into the kind of ambiguous, entropic arrangement that has become his signature — less a single narrative than a set of traces and metamorphoses left for the viewer to reassemble.

This is Strömberg's third solo outing at the gallery, following object amnesic: a compost manifesto (2022) and Vertical Matter (2019), and it arrives as part of a wider group of Berlin Art Week openings clustering around September 10.

shows.title: Transit
shows.description:
Haleh Redjaian works across drawing, textile and installation, building compositions from repeated geometric gestures — grids, arcs and interlocking lines drawn or stitched with an almost meditative discipline. Her work draws loosely on the visual vocabulary of textile pattern and architectural ornament without illustrating either directly, instead using repetition and controlled variation to produce surfaces that feel both rigorously constructed and quietly handmade.

"Transit," her exhibition at kajetan, continues this practice of patient accumulation, with a title that suggests movement, passage and the incremental buildup of form over time — a fitting frame for an artist whose work is fundamentally about process made visible. Redjaian has shown at kajetan before, and this exhibition extends her ongoing exploration of how simple, repeated marks can accrue into complex spatial rhythms.

The show opens during Berlin Art Week, with the gallery keeping extended weekend hours for the occasion — a good moment to catch Redjaian's exacting, slow-built work alongside the wider gallery activity around Charlottenburg that week.

shows.title: the Mobilisation / Poprade
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists only "From 10.09.2026" with an opening date; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Chicks on Speed — the long-running, shape-shifting art-music collective founded in the 1990s — bring their brand of DIY performance, costume and noise-pop provocation to Ebensperger's Fichtebunker space as part of Berlin Art Week. Known as much for confrontational live performance and self-produced fashion as for records, the group's gallery presentations tend to function as extensions of their stage practice: props, banners, textiles and video documentation standing in for, or feeding back into, performance.

Titled "the Mobilisation / Poprade," the show leans into the group's long-standing interest in parade, protest and pop spectacle as overlapping forms — the kind of loud, collaged, feminist-punk aesthetic Chicks on Speed have deployed since exhibitions and performances in the early 2000s. Expect a maximalist, multi-media installation rather than a conventional hang of discrete objects.

For a gallery whose program otherwise leans toward painting, drawing and film, this is a noisier, more performative entry — a good fit for Ebensperger's history of mixing visual art with music, theater and cinema under one roof.

shows.title: Bonnie Camplin Archive (BCA)
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists only "From 13.09.2026" with an opening date; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Bonnie Camplin, the British artist and a founding tutor of Goldsmiths' influential "Fine Art" cohort, turns her long-term archive of drawings, notes and research material into the exhibition itself. Camplin's practice — shortlisted for the Turner Prize in 2015 — has always treated drawing and documentation as forms of open inquiry into consciousness, belief systems and unexplained phenomena rather than as illustration, and this show reads as a rare chance to see that working method laid bare rather than distilled into finished pieces.

Camplin has shown with Ebensperger since the gallery's Berlin days at the former crematorium in Wedding, and past presentations there — like "Holographic Universe" with Beatrice Brown — have paired her intricate, systems-based drawings with collaborative and research-driven elements. This archive presentation continues that thread, offering a denser, more process-oriented counterpart to her exhibited bodies of work.

It's a good opportunity to see the connective tissue behind an artist whose finished drawings can seem hermetic — the raw material of years of looking, noting and cross-referencing, assembled as its own kind of artwork.

shows.title: Poems for Helicopter Blades
shows.artist: Fiona Banner aka The Vanity Press
shows.description:
Fiona Banner's eighth solo show with the gallery turns decommissioned military aircraft into a set of sound and video sculptures that visitors quite literally have to walk through. A helicopter blade inscribed with a text describing the Bayeux Tapestry — which Banner calls "the first ever war film" — bisects the entrance; deeper in, the melted-down aluminium of a Jaguar jet from her 2010 Tate Britain installation "Harrier and Jaguar" reappears as sculpture and picture frames, some doubling as publications registered under their own ISBN numbers.

Banner has spent decades interrogating the language and iconography of military hardware by draining it of function and reframing it through text, performance and the body — here that includes a new film, "La Fin / Runway," built from a 2021 Vogue Korea shoot in which the artist, her daughter and a model pose as fighter aircraft and birds of prey, and a soundtrack recorded on a mirror-polished jet tail-fin that reworks passages of Swan Lake. Smaller works, including sliced rotor-blade paintings and a new photogravure titled "Flypast," extend the same tension between weapon and image, body and language, that has defined her practice since the 1990s.

It's a dense, physically imposing show for a mid-size gallery space, and one of the more ambitious presentations of Banner's recent sculptural work in Berlin.

shows.title: Carrie Mae Weems
shows.description:
Carrie Mae Weems' fourth show with the gallery centers on water and migration as forces that shape identity and memory. In her "Seaside" series, the artist photographs herself from behind on a single beach, seated at an easel and facing the Atlantic — pages of her sketchbook lifting in the wind as she tries, and visibly fails, to render the ocean's scale, a quiet staging of the limits of representation in the face of historical trauma.

"The Law of Diminishing Returns" pairs that gesture with something more intimate: five oval-framed photographs, sized and composed like nineteenth-century portrait miniatures, that evoke the passage of bodies across the ocean from the transatlantic slave trade to present-day economic displacement. Both bodies of work are in direct conversation with "The Long Goodbye," a film Weems made for the opening of the V&A East in London earlier this year, and the show opens alongside her travelling survey "The Heart of the Matter" at C/O Berlin during Berlin Art Week — giving Berlin two concurrent, complementary views of one of the most consequential photographers of the past four decades.

Weems has spent her career using photography, text and installation to hold historical violence and personal tenderness in the same frame, and this show's small scale is deceptive — the miniature format asks for the kind of close, sustained looking that her subject matter demands.

shows.title: Bad Dreams
shows.description:
Susan Hiller spent much of her five-decade career treating the unconscious as raw material — collecting other people's dreams, automatic writing, séance photographs, and the debris of pop culture, then reassembling them into installations that ask what a culture's discarded or dismissed material reveals about it. Bad Dreams, billed as the first survey of her work in Berlin, is a fitting place to stage that inquiry: Hiller lived and worked in the city for several years in the early 2000s, and the exhibition draws on hypnotic, phantasmagorical audiovisual pieces alongside sculptures built from collected domestic objects and imagery scavenged from the internet, film and television.

Hiller, who died in 2019, was a trained anthropologist before she became an artist, and that background shows in the way her work treats belief systems, superstition and mass media as evidence rather than nonsense. Pieces built around recorded psychic phenomena, home movies or found photographs sit alongside more sculptural installations, all circling the same question: how do private and collective fantasies get formed, stored and passed around within ordinary cultural artifacts?

Curated by Emma Enderby and Liberty Adrien with assistant curator Lara Scherrieble, the show promises to be a rare chance to see the range of Hiller's work — spanning film, video, painting, photography, sculpture and writing — brought together in one place, and a useful reminder of how influential her strategies of appropriation and reassembly have been on younger generations of conceptual artists.

shows.title: OUSSSEAN
shows.description:
KOO JEONG A works with the barely-there: scent, light, temperature, sugar, magnets, a shaft of sun through a window — materials chosen less for what they look like than for what they do to a room. OUSSSEAN, her first major solo show in Germany, brings together key pieces from across several decades of a practice that treats architecture, sculpture, drawing, sound and even augmented reality as ways of making the intangible perceptible, drawing as much on Taoist philosophy and the traditional five elements — earth, fire, metal, water, wood — as on contemporary art history.

Reconfigured specifically for KW's building, the exhibition is less a retrospective than an atmosphere: modest, enigmatic objects and interventions distributed through the space so that visitors register them as much through the body — smell, temperature, a change in light — as through the eye. KOO, who lived in Berlin through the 1990s and 2000s before the city became a fixture in her biography, has described her interest in states that sit just below ordinary perception, and this show is designed to slow visitors down enough to notice them.

Curated by Emma Enderby and Liberty Adrien with assistant curator Lara Scherrieble, OUSSSEAN is a rare opportunity to see a substantial body of work by an artist better known internationally than locally — and a good match for KW's recent interest in art that resists easy documentation or reproduction.

shows.title: The City and the City
shows.description:
Rafik Greiss's first institutional solo show centers on a newly commissioned film, conceived as a kind of cinematic essay that drifts through Cairo, Alexandria, the Western Desert and other Egyptian sites — inhabited tombs, museum halls, open landscapes — without settling into a single narrative thread. Built from fragments, accelerations, pauses and returns, the film treats memory as something that surfaces, erodes and flickers back rather than sitting fixed, and keeps circling questions of who gets to witness or remember a place, and how history solidifies even as it wavers between fact and fiction.

Greiss, born in 1997, works across different temporalities and media, and is drawn to states of transience — the moment just before something disappears rather than its aftermath. That interest in half-visibility and afterimage carries through the whole show, which unfolds as much through mood and rhythm as through explicit argument.

Curated by Emma Enderby and Liberty Adrien with assistant curator Lara Scherrieble, and supported by the Institut français, the exhibition marks a significant platform for a young artist working at the intersection of personal recollection and collective Egyptian history — territory that recent film-based practice from the region has been exploring with increasing urgency.

shows.title: Animals
shows.description:
A group photography show built around the animal as subject, ranging from wildlife and pastoral scenes to more staged or symbolic uses of creatures in the frame. Given Galerie Springer's roster of landscape and documentary photographers, expect large-format color prints — flamingos on a Kenyan lake, donkeys in the Sicilian hills, horses and other working or wild animals caught in specific places and light rather than in a studio setting.

As a program note, the show leans on the gallery's long-standing interest in photographers who treat landscape and its inhabitants as a slow, accumulating documentary project rather than a single iconic image — so it's worth approaching this less as a themed novelty show and more as a chance to see how several different photographic eyes handle the same basic subject: animals in their environments.

shows.title: Hal Busse. Werk und Wirken
shows.description:
Timed to what would have been Hal Busse's 100th birthday, this show brings a Hamburg-originated retrospective to Berlin alongside a newly published biography of the artist. Born Hannelore Bendixen-Busse in 1926, she was one of the few women aligned with the postwar ZERO group, exhibiting alongside Otto Piene and Heinz Mack, and her work of the late 1950s and 1960s moved restlessly between painting, nail reliefs, cube progressions and architectural "Kunst am Bau" commissions.

The works on view trace that arc: taut, monochrome nail reliefs and hard-edged structural paintings from 1958-59 that put her squarely in dialogue with Concrete Art and early Kinetic art, executed in the reduced palette and serial logic typical of the ZERO circle. It's a chance to see a genuinely under-recognized figure of German postwar abstraction — someone whose sculptural objects and reliefs held their own against her better-known male ZERO contemporaries but who has only recently begun receiving retrospective attention.

Presented during Berlin Art Week, the show doubles as a launch for the accompanying monograph, which draws on the artist's own archive to reconstruct a career that ran from Stuttgart academy training under Willi Baumeister's circle through to a late-career return to landscape painting.

shows.title: Be Real.
shows.dates_note: Venue's own exhibitions page (reitergalleries.com/en/exhibitions/upcomming/) lists "Hans Aichinger — Be Real." with 2026-dated works as the gallery's next Berlin show, but publishes no exact opening/closing dates; the gallery's contact page notes it is by-appointment-only "from 22 August to 10 September," implying an opening around Sep 10, 2026 (Berlin Art Week).
shows.description:
Hans Aichinger's paintings sit in the narrow zone between recognizable figures and their dissolution — solitary, mostly adolescent subjects posed against indeterminate backdrops with a stray prop (a stick, a stuffed animal, a pebble) standing in for a scene partner. Trained in Leipzig under Bernhard Heisig, Aichinger paints with a controlled, glazed precision that pushes his figures toward abstraction the closer you look, so that a face or a torso can start to come apart into passages of pure paint even as the overall image reads as sharply legible from a distance.

Be Real gathers new oil-on-canvas works from 2026 continuing this exploration of adolescent self-possession and quiet unease — figures caught mid-gesture, neither performing nor at rest, holding a tension the artist has spent decades refining. It's a good entry point into Aichinger's work for anyone who hasn't seen his paintings before: the images are immediate and psychologically loaded even before you notice how strange the surrounding space actually is.

shows.title: Collection #4
shows.dates_note: Site lists this as the current collection presentation (URL-tagged "2022–2026", the fourth rotation since the bunker opened to the public); it is confirmed on view now but no exact opening or closing date is published.
shows.description:
The Boros bunker's fourth rotation pulls a fresh cut from Christian and Karen Boros's holdings of international art made since 1990, spread across the raw concrete floors of their converted WWII air-raid shelter in Mitte. Expect the collection's now-familiar mix of registers: moody figurative painting (Tomma Abts, Conny Maier, Louis Fratino, Jill Mulleady), sculptural and installation work that plays off the bunker's scarred walls and low ceilings (Klara Lidén, Kitty Kraus, Paloma Varga Weisz, Mire Lee), and photography and video that leans into psychological unease (Ed Atkins, Jeremy Shaw, Sung Tieu).

What distinguishes this edition is its generational spread — pairing artists who have anchored the collection for years with newer names like Lukas Heerich, Samuel Hindolo, Grant Falardeau and Rim Park, several still early in gallery representation. The result reads less like a survey than a set of private enthusiasms, exactly the point of a collection show that has never pretended to be encyclopedic.

Visits are only possible on a timed, guided tour (1.5 hours, small groups, German or English), which is unusual for a contemporary art space of this scale and worth planning around — the guides also cover the building's history as a Nazi-era bunker, techno club and finally private museum, which is as much a part of the experience as the art itself.

venue.name: Sammlung Boros (Boros Collection)
hours: Guided tours Tue - Sun, times vary by booking

shows.title: ENCOUNTERS — On Bodies, Borders, Resistance
shows.description:
Tanja Ostojić has spent more than two decades using her own body as a testing ground for questions of migration, borders and belonging, often through provocative, deliberately uncomfortable performances that expose how citizenship and mobility are policed. This survey-style exhibition at Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanien gathers work spanning her career, tracing a throughline from early performances that satirized marriage-for-papers schemes to later projects addressing the militarization of European borders.

Ostojić, who was born in the former Yugoslavia and has lived as a migrant artist across Europe, works in a mode that's equal parts conceptual art and activist intervention — her pieces frequently involve real bureaucratic processes, real border crossings, real risk, rather than staged simulations. The result is a body of work that resists easy aestheticization even as it uses performance, photography and documentation with real formal precision.

Coming right after the venue's After Memory group show, this solo exhibition continues Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanien's pattern of pairing socially engaged group projects with more sustained looks at single practices — in this case, one of the sharpest artists working on the politics of the body and the border in Europe today.

shows.title: This!
shows.description:
Schiefe Zähne closes out the summer with a seven-artist group show titled simply This!, bringing together gallery regular Matthias Groebel — the German painter known for the airbrushed, TV-still-derived canvases he has produced since the early 1990s — with Evan Jose, Morag Keil, Julian Krause, Paul Niedermayer, Niklas Taleb and Hélène Yamba-Guimbi.

The gallery has paired the show with an audio excerpt from Gretchen Bender's 1988 sound piece "Artificial Treatment," a fitting nod given Bender's own preoccupation with media saturation and image overload — concerns that resonate with Groebel's screen-grab paintings and, presumably, with the sensibility of the younger artists on the checklist. Morag Keil in particular has built a reputation on prickly, media-literate installation and video work, suggesting the show leans into questions of image circulation, authorship and attention rather than offering a single unifying medium.

As a discontinuous, loosely themed group show rather than a monographic statement, This! continues the gallery's pattern of pairing its represented artists with an international guest list for tightly scheduled, five-week runs — worth catching for the Groebel alone, but also a chance to see how a small Potsdamer Straße gallery reads the current mood among a wider generation of artists.

shows.title: This Time Tomorrow
shows.description:
Jordy Kerwick is a genuinely unlikely art-world success story — a self-taught, Melbourne-born painter who only picked up a brush in 2016 and has since built a body of work that trades in a loose, folkloric menagerie of animals, masks, and domestic clutter rendered in candy-bright oil and acrylic. This is his first Berlin solo show with König Galerie, staged in the atmospheric, half-buried Vault beneath St. Agnes, the gallery's brutalist former-church home in Kreuzberg.

The title borrows from The Kinks' 1970 song of the same name, and that lyric's shrug toward an uncertain future runs through the paintings on view. Kerwick works from small, specific details — a burst of magenta, the glint of water, a half-remembered domestic scene — and lets them accumulate into denser, stranger tableaux where the everyday tips into myth. Stripes, dots, and repeated marks give the surfaces a nervous, handmade energy; recurring hybrid creatures and masks turn straightforward still lifes into something closer to fable.

It's an unpretentious, colour-forward show, and a good example of König's willingness to mix outsider-adjacent, market-driven painters like Kerwick alongside its more conceptually rigorous program. Worth seeing in tandem with the building itself: the Vault's raw concrete and low light do a lot of work in making Kerwick's saturated palette feel almost theatrical.

shows.title: Bittersweet Symphony
shows.description:
This two-person photography show pairs a personal reckoning with a documentary portrait, both circling alcohol addiction from opposite ends of intimacy. Stefanie Moshammer works from the inside, building a fragmented body of photographs, objects and video around her mother's drinking — the material moves between closeness and withdrawal, control and vulnerability, without resolving into a tidy narrative arc. Eric Meier comes at the subject from outside, photographing men in recovery housing in Eisenhüttenstadt whose lives were shaped by the ruptures of the post-reunification years; his pictures avoid the voyeuristic angle that this kind of subject invites, working instead through proximity and restraint.

Curated by Katharina Schilling, the show deliberately declines to synthesize its two positions into a single message. It sits with shame, care and responsibility as separate, sometimes contradictory territories, and lets the poetic and the documentary modes argue with each other rather than agree.

It's a quietly difficult show, more about looking someone in the eye than about aesthetic payoff, and it's worth catching the artist talk on September 12 if the timing works, since both photographers will be present to unpack how differently they approached the same wound.

shows.title: Dropping In and Out – A Response to Uncertainty
shows.description:
This research-driven group show grew out of a collaboration between artists Mathilde ter Heijne and Vanessa Gravenor (both at the UdK Berlin) and literary scholar Jessica Goodman at Oxford, and it's structured less like a conventional exhibition than an act of collective biography-writing. Two dozen historical women — some well documented, most nearly erased from the record — are each taken up by a contemporary artist or researcher and given a fragmentary, personal portrait built from letters, archival research, film and multimedia work.

The cast of historical subjects is deliberately eclectic: the revolutionary-era writer Marie-Jeanne Roland, who used her final weeks before execution to write her own account of her life; the photographer Zofia Rydet, who didn't pick up a camera seriously until her forties and went on to become one of Poland's most important image-makers; the economist and psychologist Dora Benjamin, who curated a 1929 Kreuzberg exhibition on the psychological toll of labor and city life. Rather than smoothing these lives into inspirational narratives, the artists lean into the gaps, ruptures and career interruptions — illness, war, migration, care work — that don't fit the usual success-story template.

The opening on September 18 kicks off a program that includes a performative reading by UdK performance students and a later evening of film screenings with several of the participating artists in conversation. Worth catching for anyone interested in feminist historiography or in watching artists work through archival material in real time rather than presenting it as a finished argument.

shows.title: Solo Show
shows.dates_note: Gallery page lists 31 October – 4 December 2026; press text notes the opening is 30 October.
shows.description:
Dutch painter Ab van Hanegem returns to the gallery for a solo presentation of new acrylic paintings and works on paper. Van Hanegem, trained at St. Joost in Breda and the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, works in a loose, gestural abstraction that often edges toward figuration — bodies, viscera, and landscape forms surface and dissolve again in scraped and layered passages of acrylic, occasionally cut with coal or charcoal.

His paintings have a rawness that comes from working fast and revising in the open: pentimenti and drips are left visible, and the palette swings between chalky pastels and sudden, almost bruised darks. Van Hanegem has shown at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam and the Van Abbemuseum Eindhoven among other institutions, and this show continues a long-running relationship with the gallery that dates back over a decade.

Expect a mix of larger canvases and more intimate paper works, giving a good sense of how his mark-making shifts in scale — tighter and more graphic on paper, looser and more atmospheric on canvas.
